p: Okay. We've heard many examples of projects where city reimbursement can take years. Can you explain the process for approving reimbursements and why that sometimes can take years after project completion. And I actually have one example of that which is the David Geffen Hall, which opened October 8th, 2022. Lincoln Center is still waiting for DDC to complete payment on the project. Also Carnegie Hall is accruing $2 million in interest each year for capital projects. So, yeah, what is the plan supporting these institutions and making sure institutions are paid on time and do not face increased interest rates or impacts on their credit ratings?

Yeah, Councilmember. So, in prepping for this hearing, this issue came up. I think the bigger issue is the coordination between us and the cultural institution. A lot of this work happens before a contract's even registered. And so the city cannot— doesn't even have the ability to pay until the contract is registered. So you mentioned the Geffen Hall at Lincoln Center. The contract you

mentioned, the work was done in 2022. The contract wasn't registered until September 2024. From there we had meetings up until end of 2024. We were still going back and forth with Lincoln Center about some documents that were missing for us to be able to make the payment. I understand that on paper it sounds really frustrating, but if an institution is doing work ahead of contract registration, the city doesn't even have the ability to pay. And so we understand that sometimes that needs to happen and the timelines are tight, but I would really encourage them to work with us to make sure that at least they know the expectations up front. And in this case, it's not like they've been waiting for a payment for a number of years, as I think on paper it would show, it's that we didn't actually register the contract until very—
[interposing] But why? Can you help me understand why contracts—

[interposing] Yeah, so the way– the way that it would work is essentially we get– the capital grant process may not be in place ahead of them, of the institution wanting to do work, but they have the commitment, the funding commitment

in place. And so they're making the decisions to make the repairs or renovations with the funding commitment, but not with the capital grant fully registered with the Comptroller. And so there's a bit of a disconnect. I think this is a very good topic for us to discuss.
Yeah, because like, but why? Why does it take so long to register the contract?

So, I don't know the full details. I don't know if it's we're not getting all the right information. I– this is a very good topic if we are going to host a roundtable to discuss because I want to be upfront with the cultural institutions about the expectations of doing that work at risk without a fully registered contract. I understand that the— that means that their projects are not going to start as fast as they would like, but it does avoid delays on the back end. And so–
[interposing] Yeah, it’s like, damn if you do, damn if you don't, because, like, if they don't start it, then, like, that can lead to, like, a whole bunch of— an array of issues.
Sure.

Maybe the project cost goes up, maybe they have disruptions in their programs or their performances. But then now when they do it, you're like, oh well, you did it, and now you got to wait until we catch up with the bureaucracy.
I think you’re–
[interposing] Like, I don't—
[interposing] You're bringing up a very good point.
That’s crazy.
And also, you know, a lot of these cultural institutions are, you know, taking out bridge loans to make sure that they're—
[interposing] Yeah, now they're paying interest on loans.

That's right. Yes. It's not an easy solution. I think being upfront about the risk-benefit of doing that is important, and you have my commitment to really make sure at least to– for the cultural institutions to know

exactly what they're getting into if they are going to be doing work, what we consider work at risk.
Yeah, I think transparency is important, but I also think– thinking of not just like a Band-Aid, because I think transparency is just like band-aiding the problem–
[interposing] Yeah.

but like really trying to find a cure for the disease as to like why it takes so long to register a contract, especially when that cultural institution is— sounds like self-managing. That's like– that is when we really should be helping the cultural institution by, like, at the very least, registering the contract so you can get paid.

I would say, Council Member, it is not just the cultural institution at times that's missing documents. It could be the contractor not provide— there's like the request for– like, the city has to approve subcontractors. Sometimes there's like PLAs or other labor things that need to be involved. And so it is a very burdensome process. It is required by spending city dollars. I want my city dollars to be spent on

prevailing wage and sort of your typical– what it comes with spending a city dollar. But I agree with you, and I understand that frustration. And Commissioner?

No, I just want to echo, of course we understand the frustration that cultural organizations are experiencing with this. And both Commissioner and myself are quite new here and have our first meeting actually scheduled next week so we can begin coordinating better and be able to communicate these unique specific challenges, because DCLA works so differently than other sister agencies. So, yes, we understand and we are in conversation about—

Thank you. Institutions are foregoing city processes for procuring equipment. It takes too long, and items will often be out of warranty by the time they arrive. Often SIGs will wait until they can afford the entire equipment replacement privately. What are the primary holdups for equipment projects, and what is being done to streamline equipment projects?

So, I will say that over the past several years, we've been able to

reduce our equipment procurement timeline by six months. I— we haven't heard— we've only heard one case of equipment being delivered out of warranty. So that is not something that we've heard before, but—
I'm sure the cultural institutions will share, as I'm looking at faces and they're smiling and laughing. So I'm sure there are more cases, but so yeah, hopefully somebody can stay back–
[interposing] I’m happy to listen to all of them.

yeah, from DCLA to hear the testimony. Okay, no worries. So we can circle back to that. DCLA has not updated the capital project tracker as we discussed, or as I mentioned in my opening, since 2021. The tracker is required by local law. Why hasn't it been updated, and can you commit to updating the tracker?
Yeah, data transparency is incredibly important to us. This just came to my attention last week, and as of today, the data is updated.

That's why we have hearings, oversight, transparency. We love it. Thank

you. Okay. Advocates and cultural organizations are calling for a cultural capital plan, a systemic citywide framework for assessing the condition of city-owned cultural assets and budgeting sensibly for state of good repair, modernization, and energy efficiency projects, along with expansion projects. Is there anything that would prevent DCLA from establishing and maintaining such a plan? If not, are you committed to a five-year capital plan? And I know you mentioned, when I asked the question about do you assess buildings, that you do feel this could be potentially used to create a plan. So, yes. Is there anything that would preclude you from doing it? And if not, you know, are you able to commit to doing a capital plan?

I'm definitely looking forward to talking to the CIGs about this. I haven't received any details about what the proposal is, but have started the conversation with them already. Looking forward to learning more.

Okay. And just a few questions, not cultural or library— libraries related, but MWBEs, unless the Chair— do you plan to ask questions on MWBEs? Okay. I'm very passionate

about MWBEs, and so– and I know Chair Restler is as well, and there's a set of MWBE questions. The Public Works Investment Act requires project labor agreements for alternative delivery contracts, and DDC has reported that minority and women-owned business enterprise utilization on design-build and CM-Build projects has been higher than on low-bid contracts, with participation goals of 30 percent for both the design and construction phases. How does MWBE participation rates compare across design-builds, progressive design-builds, CM-Build and traditional low-bid contracts?

Yeah, Council Member, we share your support and passion for MBEs. It was something that I championed with former Commissioner Rodriguez at DOT, and it's something that our Executive Deputy Commissioner Maggie Austin at DDC really, really cares about and has done a fantastic job at increasing participation. We have found that MWBE participation is much easier in design-build projects, just because the goals are desegregated, which means essentially there's, like, an ability to bring in more subcontractors of smaller size. Let me just give you an example. The Shirley Chisholm Rec

Center had an MWBE participation of over 30 percent— 33— 36 percent, which has been the highest MWBE participation rate that we've ever had. And that's the– that's the goal, essentially making it easier for smaller firms, which MWBE firms tend to be smaller, for them to have access to contracting opportunities. It is something that we're very proud. I think our BBJ program is doing exactly that. We hope to get about 30 percent MWBE participation across all the contracts in our BBJ program. Oh, I would– and compared to design bid build, the reason why the percentages aren't as high as design bid build is because the contracts are not segregated. And so you have one preliminary design, one final design, and one construction. We do have goals, but it's much harder to exercise the tools of using subs or nudging contractors to use MWBE subs.
How does a PLA affect project delivery, workforce stability, and opportunities for city residents?

Yeah, it doesn't affect them. We believe it enhances them. It is essentially a PLA is sort of setting the rules of the game ahead of the project. Everything from wage—

wages to deliveries and conflict resolution and sort of everything that you need ahead of the project to start. We have them in design-build projects as part of the— Yes, as part of the state law, they're required in horizontal and vertical design-build projects. It's been working great. I– we also have a community hiring component, which was also approved by state law. I am happy to dive a little deeper on that. If we have some metrics, I would love to share them. The opportu— the goal here is to hire local residents into these jobs and ideally bring them into trades for them to have a path towards a good– a well-paid union job.
Yeah, like actually getting into the trades because sometimes they do the apprenticeship–
[interposing] Apprenticeship, yeah.

pipeline, which isn't actually like getting them into the trade. So we try to encourage, like, them actually getting into the trade so it isn't just like the one project in their community, but that they can take their, like, now union card and go to another project. We just

want to make sure that faster project delivery doesn't compromise or come at the expense of inclusion or accountability. So—
I think that's right, and it hasn't yet, and I have no reason to believe it will.
Okay, thank you so much, Chairs.

Thank you, Chair Restler. The report also— this referring to the Comptroller's report, I'm going— I'm back to the report– found that when calculating the extent of project delays, DDC does not count certain delays as delays. The report states that DDC, and I quote, “unilaterally excludes all delays it considers outside of its control. As a result, the MMR does not provide a complete picture of the delays that occur. In the MMR, DDC excludes time added to the project duration due to changes in programmatic scope and delays it considers beyond its control.” Why does DDC exclude these delays from its delay calculations?

Yeah, I mean, the— but by mere fact of the statement, it's a DDC delay, I wouldn't consider those DDC delays. But I

understand your point, and it goes back to sort of like understanding a baseline of what is a delay. I think we can have a philosophical discussion of what is delay, but for the public it doesn't really matter. So I— a point well taken.
I appreciate you saying that because at the end of the day, I feel like we're all just trying to convince ourselves we're doing a good job.
Yes.
But the members of the public–
[interposing] That’s right.
are, you know, it's delayed, so–
[interposing] I would say though, they will enjoy the scoping changes that come from that. But I— point well taken, I don't think the public cares, and I'm happy to look into it to see if there's—

[interposing] Yeah, I think— and I'm happy to move away from the delay discussion, except there may be another one. The

Comptroller's report also states, and I quote, “DDC contracts frequently require mid-project adjustments due to this added scope, unforeseen underground conditions, or delayed utility responses. However, the audit's review of project records and sampled project files suggests that in many cases delays categorized as external, for example, field conditions or scope changes, and therefore deemed unavoidable by DDC, may stem from avoidable causes such as design omissions, or insufficient project readiness.” Given that DDC is involved in establishing and changing the scope of any project, why does DDC classify design omissions or insufficient project readiness as outside of the agency's control?

Chair, I would like to see those examples, because I— if it's a design omission, it would— it should have been caught at the front end planning. That's the whole purpose of that unit. But if it's a change in scope, that's not a design omission. That is a design— like, it's increasing the scope. And so I would love to talk to my team about the specific examples that the Comptroller pointed out. I would say, though, I keep

saying it, we don't know what is under our streets, especially in Manhattan. We— the utilities don't have a good grasp. They have an idea, and we try to ask to try to get– we try as much as we can to anticipate what will be underground, but it's very hard. And so we don't know exactly what's down there until we, you know, rip up the streets. And so it does—
[interposing] You mean to tell me you can't see through cement?
Unforeseen field conditions unfortunately are unavoidable at times.
Got it. I just want us to redefine, right, what a delay is. I think that's something that we have to have a meeting of the minds on.
Sure.

So that when my constituents are coming up to me or the folks of the city are coming up to me and saying, how is this not a delay? And I'm like, it is a delay. It's just not a delay for agency term— agencies that want to make themselves feel a little better.
[inaudible] about scoping changes and front-end planning, if you would like.

Alright, I have questions for DOT, and I'm going to get to the one that my constituents really, really care about, and I know that I have plenty of them here. I see Anne, I see Jack Fogel. Is there other folks? And Lynette. These are folks who have had to live— these are folks who live in my building, by the way. And these are folks who keep me accountable, and I told them to show up today, so I'm very proud of them for coming up and holding me accountable. It's getting to the point where even the— even my doorman is asking me about the status of projects from the city. Seriously. And I'm like, man, everybody's coming after me. So now is the time to ask these questions, and I'm glad that you're going to be here to testify later. In 2019, Judd Law began work on the Riverside Drive Viaduct project to repair corroding steel and decking along the elevated portion of the drive as part of a contract worth over $100 million. Work has eventually stopped. Folks from Judd Law have walked off the project for over a year, leaving behind an

unfinished construction site that disrupts the lives of people in this neighborhood. It is a blight. I look outside my window, the residents of my building look outside this window, folks from 153rd to 161st, they look outside of their windows and they have to live with this nightmare. What happened with this project?

First off, Majority Leader, thank you for your advocacy on this project and all the other projects in your district. I want to say first and foremost, we're in active litigation with Judd Law on this project. We wanted to move forward with a default of the contractor, but we're given a temporary restraining order by the judge. We want to move forward, we want to complete the project, we want to see the residents of your district and the folks in your building happy and not clamoring for projects to finish. As Commissioner Ochoa said, you know, the delays are one of the things that, you know, bother all of us most. We hope to have a resolution soon. We'll continue conversations with the contractor and litigation and hope to get to a resolution soon.

Thank you for that update on the temporary restraining order. That is news to me, and I think that indicates– you know, I have to say that under the Mamdani administration, there's been a lot of active efforts to find a resolution here, in a way that, you know, the past administration didn't have a sense of urgency. And so I just want to say thank you for providing us with this update, potentially moving for default if you can. And the TRO shows that at least something is happening and I have something to report back. Is it permissible for a contractor to walk off a project while there is a dispute about costs?

We do our absolute best to make sure that we can come to an amenable solution with contractors. Of course, things happen that are outside any of our controls. Many of our contractors are firms we've worked with before, so we want to make sure that we can continue working with them. And if things happen, like they walk off the job, you know, we have things in the contract that we will have to exercise. And, you know, we look at things on a case-by-case basis.

I mean– I mean I would suspect that it would not be permissible for a contractor to just walk off a project. But I understand that the city is holding them accountable by moving forward with enforcing the terms of the contract through the default proceeding.
Yes.
And so I hope that that pressure stays on. Does the city have a timeline for work resuming on this project, or is that all that contingent on the resolution of this default, etcetera?

Unfortunately, it's all tied to the resolution. We'd like to move forward with a different contractor and get the project done, but unfortunately this TRO kind of puts us at an impasse. I do want to say that we're not sitting on our hands and just waiting for the TRO to finish. We're trying to move forward and looking for any and all possible solutions to move forward.
And you— and under the contract, you would be able to find another vendor through a surety bond? Is that how that would work?
Let me get back to you.

Yep. No problem. Will the work on this project— let's assume that there is a default and that the city succeeds with that, would that affect Judd Law's standing when they bid for future city projects?
Yes, it would.

Is there— it would. Okay, that's good to know. And is there existing laws that says that if there is a prior default, that's a factor that the agency is required to consider as part of granting future projects?
So from a big picture standpoint, any and all contracts get grades after the project is complete. We factor those grades in when we're reviewing contractors for future work.

Good. Alright, well, that's music to my ears, because I feel like for a very long time, Judd Law has been operating as if they're too big to fail and that they have this leverage over the city and the state, having billions

of dollars in public service contracts. It has been of huge concern. I know they also have another contract on 79th Street, for instance, as well. They have a lot of state contracts with the MTA. If Judd Law is paying attention, I hope you are paying attention, we're coming after you. You have an obligation to do right by the city and do right by the contract terms. And if you don't, yes, you may get defaulted, and that's going to impact future projects. It's going to impact your ability to do business with the city, because the residents of my district, the residents of this city deserve better. You imagine you're building a bridge, and all of a sudden you decide to walk off the— walk off the job? But you know what? They're mistreating the residents of uptown Manhattan by walking off. You guys can reserve your rights in court, through litigation and still complete the project. And then after that, litigate the cases on the merits, and you reserve your rights to do that. You should not make sure— you should not, at the expense of my constituents, wait for them for that project to be done. It's been seven years. Well, we have a stranded road. It's not right. And so I just want to say thank you so much to the

Chairs. I have no other questions on this matter. I want to thank the Commissioner for testifying in good faith.

Thank you. I— just before letting this panel go, I just— I did want to underscore to Commissioner Ochoa, I think that there was some good work over the last year in expanding underground mapping efforts. And, you know, I think it's so important that the utility companies work collaboratively with us, that National Grid and Con Ed are held accountable to share transparently their information, and that we're all mapping it, DEP's infrastructure, their infor— the utility infrastructure, so that when work is happening, we can consolidate projects as much as possible. There is nothing that annoys our constituents more, the people of New York City more, that when the same street gets dug up three times in a one-year span because Con Ed, Nat Grid, DEP, DOT, nobody's talking to one another or cares what anyone else is doing. And the utility companies in particular, I think, have zero you know what's to give. So how we bring them to the table and hold them accountable is really important. With that, I want to thank you all for

testifying today. We really appreciate your thoughtful testimony.
Thank you.

Hope you all have a wonderful afternoon and congratulations to the new commissioners once again, and happy birthday. Alright, we're going to first bring up the libraries. So we'll bring up and forgive me if I can't read anyone's handwriting, David Lam from NYPL, Karen Sheehan from BPL, and John Katimaris from Queens Public Library, QPL. Okay, you all feel free to testify in whatever order you would so like, and the clock will start whenever the first one begins. Yeah, and could one of the sergeants— would you mind closing the doors just so we can get some of the noise from outside? Thank you.

Good afternoon, my name is David Lam, and I am the Vice President for Capital Planning and Construction at the New York Public Library. I would like to thank Speaker Julie Menin, Chairs Dr. Natasha Williams, Lincoln Restler, and Sean Abreu, the committee members, and the entire City Council for holding this hearing. NYPL's 92 locations across the Bronx, Manhattan, and Staten

Island are integral community hubs offering free access to books, computers, internet access, and programming for all ages. Capital improvements ensure that our essential services are delivered in a safe, welcoming, and accessible spaces for all our patrons and staff. NYPL's active capital portfolio as of April 2026 consists of 30 projects with a total value of over $331 million. By fiscal year 2028, we estimate that NYPL will have invested a total of $1.2 billion towards capital improvements since fiscal year 2015, including $747.1 million in city capital funding. This includes many of the street projects across our nation— across our locations, such as roofs, windows, building systems, as well as 31 comprehensive renovations and new locations, which accounts for more than one-third of our branches. And we have many highlights we can go into, but to keep within the time, I can talk to them afterwards then. We have made great progress on capital improvements across the system, but it's important to note that most of the library's recent success results from creative approaches that seek to avoid the cost escalations and lengthy timelines associated with the traditional city capital process. Finding

efficiencies ensures that we are reliable stewards of public funding and that our patrons and staff do not have to wait to see critical needs addressed in their libraries. One of these creative approaches is working with Economic Development Corporation, as we did for our five Carnegie renovation projects. These projects were completed in less than six years, even with 11-month 2020 COVID restrictions. All five branches were over 100 years old, multi-floors, involved a mix of landmark buildings, access agreements, complex regulatory process, and percent for arts projects. On the other hand, our renovation of Hamilton Fish Park in Lower Manhattan is a much simpler one-story project managed by DDC, started around the same time as the Carnegie's and experienced also the COVID pause and is still as yet to be completed. At the time the funding was secured in 2015, the library anticipated it would take four years, $8.5 million to complete. But after numerous contract amendments and extended DDC internal reviews, design was not completed until 2022. During that time, the branch's HVAC system failed, and NYPL was forced to temporarily close the branch, spend NYPL operating dollars to outfit it with temporary

heating and cooling, and reopen with limited service prior to closing again for construction in 2024. An original— a project— though– sorry. A project originally estimated to be completed in four years and cost $8.5 million will ultimately take 10 years and cost $18.5 million. We know that when we work with DDC, cost escalations are inevitable. We have incurred $54 million in shortfalls on DDC-managed projects between FY18 and '25. This directly impacts our approach to requesting new funding. Since we know shortfalls are inevitable, we must preemptively ask for contingency funding until project reaches construction. The Council has provided unallocated capital funding, which allows us to plug shortfalls and initiate emergency projects as they arise.
We'll just ask you to wrap up, please, if you can get a chance.
Okay.
Thanks so much.

We'll go through then— slide through some of them. Some of the— what we're all talking about is some of the opportunities and alternatives that we have approached to some of these because we cannot rely on the DDC and the

capital process. Some of the items that we've done is we've done library culture grants, pass-throughs where we self-manage projects. But as you mentioned, there are issues with this. We do have large outlays of cash that we have to wait for reimbursements on. And that is a— it helps— it impacts our capacity to manage other projects and continue other work.
Thank you so much. That's great. We really appreciate it. We have your full written testimony and it's submitted into the record. Thank you.

Good afternoon, Deputy Speaker, Dr. Williams, Majority Leader Abreu, Chair Restler and members of the committee. My name is Karen Sheehan, and I am the Executive Vice President for Finance and Administration at the Brooklyn Public Library. Library's capital planning, facilities management, and finance teams are among the departments that I oversee. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today. The libraries are modern time town squares, among the most democratic spaces in the city. We provide safe, welcoming environments for everyone who enters our doors. In Brooklyn last year, our

buildings hosted more than 6 million visits. But the strength of our institution, in a very literal sense, is tied to the strength of our roofs, the reliability of our boilers, and the safety and accessibility of our spaces. I want to thank this council and the mayor for your partnership. Because of your longstanding investment in our branches, Brooklyn Public Library is undergoing its most significant era of rebuilding in decades. Over a third of our branches in our system are currently under renovation or have recently been reconstructed. From the brand new Greenpoint and Sunset Park and Brooklyn Heights libraries to upcoming construction at New Lots and Canarsie, we're building world-class inspirational facilities for our patrons. However, the story of our capital success is shadowed by the growing deferred maintenance crisis. In Brooklyn, the average age of our branches is 74 years, with 20 of our 62 locations over a century old. It's no wonder that last year, BPL lost over 1,000 hours of public service to infrastructure failures. When these infrastructure failings cannot wait on for a planned capital project, we're forced to raid our operating funds to respond to these emergencies. It's the most expensive

and least efficient way to run our facilities. Building maintenance emergencies divert about a million dollars out of our operating budget every year. Every expense dollar that we spend on an emergency repair is one that we cannot spend on programming or boost our collection. BPL is a steward of over 1 million square feet of city-owned buildings while we carry a burden of more than $400 million in unfunded capital needs. Our capital crisis is in large part due to inadequate funding. Without a source of recurring unallocated capital funds, we are forced to respond to emergencies rather than plan for preventative maintenance. Over the years, the Council's lump sum capital allocation has been a lifeline, allowing us to address these urgent repairs. We're facing $12.8 million in DDC project shortfalls, and capital city– and Council's capital funding has been instrumental in helping keep us– these projects moving forward. We're very grateful for your support, and once again, we are requesting another $10 million from our Brooklyn delegation. We're also submitting a 10-year capital plan to the administration of $276 million, which will enable us to do comprehensive overhauls like we have done in

the past. Comprehensive branch renovations address multiple improvements in a single project, saving time, money, and reducing library service. We've leaned into creative solutions that BPL has taken on, on our own. We've laid it out in our written testimony. But essentially, BPL-managed projects with city capital grants that we have done over the last couple of years include co-locations with housing and cultural institutions. Currently BPL has 39 capital projects with the Department of Design and Construction, 28 active projects and 11 that are being initiated. We appreciate the efforts of the DDC team that had— that they've made to improve project management and delivery. Together, we have learned to become more deliberate in the scoping projects for greater success. They are active partners. However, we would like to note some structural issues that the city could continue to improve upon. Front-end planning unit, which we heard a lot about earlier, began as a solution to define project scope and develop more accurate cost estimates before project initiation.
We'll just ask that you wrap up when you get a chance.

Instead, it's become a lengthy, cumbersome process. So the other– so we— the procurement process for design services, legal review, and preconstruction services is extensive and is drawn out by a long bid packaging process. If some of these reviews could happen concurrently and timelines condensed, we would save time and money on our projects. If you'd like, I can stop there.
That's great. We have your testimony submitted into the record, and we do, I know, have some questions, but we'll go to Queens and then we'll ask some questions.

Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Deputy Speaker, Majority Leader, and Chair, and other members of the New York City Council. Just want to give you a fair warning, speed is not my strong point, but I will try to breeze through the written testimony and pull out some of the highlights. We have across the borough of Queens approximately 66 locations totaling just under 1 million square feet. The average vintage is just above 50 years old. Currently, we have 37 active capital projects with DDC totaling $450 million in

construction cost only, and I want to make sure everyone understands that, right? So construction cost is about 70 percent of the total funding obligation. So it's $450 million in construction cost. We also have four self-managed capital projects totaling about $21 million, again, only in terms of construction cost. Our commitment rate has been steadily improving. When I say our commitment rate, I'm talking about Queens Library specifically. And commitment rate is easily— most easily defined as the efficiency with which the planned capital budget is converted into registered contracts in a given fiscal year. So we've topped out at an 84 percent success rate at $70.7 million. So it's an— it's an efficiently run capital program in terms of this commitment rate, which is the report card that OMB tends to look at. As far as time, I just want to also state that our records show that on average, from design start to design end, on a DDC-managed conventional design-bid-build project, it's nine years. 46 percent of that time is in design, 12 percent in procurement, and 42 percent in construction. We're working with DDC to improve some of these timelines. We've created an internal

infrastructure that addresses scope, shortfalls, and standardized design. And we expect that to yield positive results in the foreseeable future. We do on occasion, in cases of urgent repairs, we have to tie into our expense— dip into our expense funds to take care of these urgent matters, primarily HVAC infrastructure. And we have on occasion involved– we've been involved with the New York City pass-through project, most recently our Bay Terrace renovation, about a $4.7 million renovation. But that has consequences in terms of cash flow and front— having to front the money. So it does have some punitive impact as far as, well, accounting and economic housekeeping. That's– now see, then that's pretty good. Maybe I should consult with DDC on finishing on time. Thank you very much for your time and attention.
Queens gets the credit for being on time. We'll start with the Majority Leader. I have a question too, but you go first. The Deputy Speaker. I just got myself confused.

It's just Nantasha at the end of the day. What was the hardest part of

dealing with the city? Which step in the process funding approvals, procurement, or reimbursement was most challenging and why?

I can take part of that question. I think what we find a lot of it is the, as you kind of mentioned, is the time delays. And also just a little bit of the rigidity of the process overall where things all have to go into sequence. Things don't work very quickly at times and it causes long delays. Good afternoon, and thank you for the opportunity to testify today. My name is John Surico, and I'm the senior fellow for Climate and Opportunity at Center for an Urban Future, an independent research organization focused on building a stronger and more equitable New York City. I'd like to begin by commending Chairs Abreu, Restler, and Williams, Council Member Krishnan, and members of the committee for focusing on an issue that rarely makes headlines but has huge consequences for New Yorkers. At a time of fiscal uncertainty, New York City needs to stretch capital dollars farther than ever before to continue delivering the vital facilities and spaces that residents rely on. This is an issue that CUF has focused on for many years. In the 2021 report stretching New York City's capital dollars, we called for every agency in office with a capital portfolio or oversight role to launch a capital project delivery blueprint, building on important work already underway at DDC. We're glad to see Intro 263

advance that same idea, and we appreciate the Council's leadership. The need is urgent. The city's parks, libraries, cultural institutions, and other vital civic infrastructure face billions of dollars in unmet state of good repair needs. And with higher interest rates constraining the city's ability to borrow, officials will need to get every drop out of our limited capital dollars. There's reason for optimism. DDC has made important progress through its strategic blueprint for capital project delivery improvements. The agency has cut the medium building project duration by 11 months since 2019 and median infrastructure project duration by 18 months while making use of faster delivery tools like design-build. The new Shirley Chisholm Rec Center in Flatbush and East Flatbush shows what's possible. Led by DDC, this new recreation facility was one of the first city projects to use design-build. The contracting method is credited with reducing the timeline by three years and shaving 10 percent off the final bill, more than $10 million in taxpayer savings. The next step is to make this approach truly system-wide. Building on DDC's progress will require streamlining every stage of the capital process, from

how elected officials fund projects to community engagement, design, procurement, construction, closeout. That means extending this blueprint to every agency that manages capital projects, including NYC Parks, DOT, as well as offices whose approvals and reviews can add months to timelines, especially OMB, including the certificate to proceed process and the Office of the New York City Comptroller. If New York is serious about building faster, reform has to reach every part of the system. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.
